extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and computer scientists writing research papers, expository articles, and textbooks (graduate students, researchers, authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and evaluative criteria for writing mathematics and computer science papers, expository pieces, and textbooks—covering presentation, exposition, examples, organization, and publication expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get the reader's attention immediately
rubrics_metrics.description: Snappy titles, arresting first sentences, and lucid initial paragraphs are methods for getting readers' attention right away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: Gleason's attention-getting title, Thurston's striking opening question, and an autobiographical first paragraph that gives immediate insight. Note: author fame helps, but strong openings still matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell everything up front (tell readers what you will do)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell your readers in plain English what you are going to write about so they can decide whether to read on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted advice: 'You can quintuple your readership if you will let them in on what it is that you are doing.' Be explicit about goals and results early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make results and theorems easy to find (readers scan)
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers scan papers looking for statements of theorems and key results; present those prominently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use boldface (or 'neon') for summaries and results; avoid heavy notational abbreviations and convoluted references inside theorem statements so skim-readers can latch on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use motivation sparingly and appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: A little motivation is good; too much will bore readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present a few motivating examples that may not yield the desired result (useful technique) but don't overuse it. Balance motivation with concise technical content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use well-chosen examples generously
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples are crucial: even simple examples convey much of the idea; follow up with more complex examples to illustrate 'grubbies'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jeff Ullman: 'I never saw a book with too many examples.' Finding examples that illustrate only the intended points takes time; invest effort to select them well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'mysteriously convenient starting points' (be transparent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like 'Consider the following...' often signal an ad-hoc or unexplained choice from left field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such constructions make readers suspect the author is sneaking in an unmotivated assumption; prefer clearly motivated constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep definitions close to their uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't define something in one place and use it many pages later; readers don't work that way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeat definitions if necessary to keep exposition usable. Avoid forcing the reader to flip back and forth between distant sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a readable proof-exposition rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: Be chatty and expository before a proof, present the proof in a 'lean and mean' rigorous style, then be chatty again after the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilf's recommended style: lead up conversationally to give intuition, keep the formal proof concise and rigorous (Rudin-style), and then return to exposition to discuss significance and extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the exposition level accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep the level of exposition low enough that intended readers can follow; don't assume too much background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tradeoffs exist when using powerful machinery: either teach the basics (spend pages) or avoid opaque shortcuts. Justify methods and avoid relying on obscure techniques without explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: State types and be referentially clear
rubrics_metrics.description: State the types of your variables and avoid non-referential uses of 'this' that leave readers bewildered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write, e.g., 'the set S' not 'S'; avoid 'this' that doesn't cite a clear referent. Clear naming and typing reduce reader confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put yourself in the reader's place
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipate what will be hard to learn and order exposition accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spend a day studying a topic and write it up that evening to get the expository order right. Use the perspective of a learner to decide explanations and repetitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use consistent and helpful typographic conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Typographic choices (fonts, notation styles) should aid readability and clarify distinctions (e.g., presenting logic in a typewriter font).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good typographic conventions were praised as part of good exposition. Consistency helps readers parse formal vs informal material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor presentation to venue: novelty vs exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: For research journals (e.g., Journal of Algorithms), papers should present results that are new, important, and significant; presentation beauty can be secondary. For expository journals (e.g., The Monthly), excellent exposition is the primary criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the novelty/importance criteria are met, some leeway in presentation is acceptable for research journals. Choose venue accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use puzzles or motivating examples to build mental structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce a problem via a puzzle or carefully chosen example to prime readers to see why an algorithm or proof might exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilf: solving a puzzle helps readers form 'exactly the right mental structures' for a problem; this can make complex algorithms more comprehensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify use of powerful machinery; avoid opacity
rubrics_metrics.description: When using advanced or powerful techniques, either teach them or justify why you invoke them; don't leave readers with opaque steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to provide the background (many pages) or to use only basic calculations and references. Prefer clarity over displaying advanced tools without explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find co-authors to filter idiosyncrasies
rubrics_metrics.description: Co-authors won't necessarily save time, but they help filter out an author's oddities and improve overall quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jeff: co-authors help prevent 'craziness' and produce a more marketable and readable textbook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analogy and metaphor judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogy and metaphor can aid exposition (as in physics texts) but should be used only when the reader will 'get the point'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious: the nature of the subject may limit the usefulness of analogy, but where helpful it can greatly illuminate concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid writing for the wrong motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't write papers merely to inflate publication lists or to secure placement in a particular conference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leslie Lamport: these bad reasons often lead to sloppy or low-value papers. Write to disseminate accurate and useful information instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful about plagiarism and imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation becomes culpable when a reasonable person could not believe you didn't have the other work open while writing; you can't copyright ideas, only expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If in doubt, quote explicitly. Identical notational choices and formatting can be damning; sequences of copied equations are clear plagiarism. Survey papers may quote more freely but be explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan books with a market and sales strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a niche (be the hardest, easiest, or best book on the subject) and plan for sales (aim for ~10,000 domestic sales to make it financially worthwhile).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare camera-ready copies to reduce publisher costs, negotiate royalties, aim for steady sales (e.g., 2,000/year), and consider co-authors to broaden appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use many examples in textbooks and reuse examples for new editions
rubrics_metrics.description: Textbooks benefit from abundant examples; second editions still take substantial work but can reuse earlier examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jeff: examples convey most of an idea; updating editions renews the sales lifecycle but take time (~a kilohour).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose clear, useful terminology and be prepared to rename
rubrics_metrics.description: Terminology and naming matter; awkward names can be regrettable, but community adoption sometimes forces changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: choices like 'daemon' vs 'oracle' or 'nematocyst' vs 'stinger' can have long-term impact. Consider clarity and community acceptance when naming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting and combinatorial formulas must yield integers — use this as a check and proof technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Combinatorial derivations should produce integer counts; if expressions don't look integer this signals interesting number-theoretic consequences (e.g., deriving Fermat's Little Theorem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use integer-ness of counting results as a consistency check and source of further mathematical insight; present such derivations clearly to show their broader implications.
